'''''Oxalis stricta''''', called the '''common yellow woodsorrel''' (or simply '''yellow woodsorrel'''), '''common yellow oxalis''', or '''upright yellow-sorrel''' is a [[herbaceous plant]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Oxalis stricta |url=https://www.robsplants.com/plants/OxaliStric |date=2004-08-02 |website=robsplants.com}}</ref>

== Habitat ==
''O. stricta'' is [[native species|native]] to [[North America]] and [[East Asia]] and has been introduced elsewhere, especially in [[Europe]].<ref name="pfaf1">{{Cite web |title=Oxalis stricta Yellow Wood Sorrel, Common yellow oxalis, Common Yellow Wood Sorrel, Oxalis PFAF Plant Database |url=https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Oxalis+stricta |access-date=2024-04-24 |website=pfaf.org}}</ref> It was not documented in Michigan before the 1890s.{{sfn|Voss|1972|p=501}}

It tends to grow in [[woodland]]s, [[meadow]]s, and in disturbed areas as both a [[perennial]] and [[annual plant|annual]].<ref name="kingdomplantae">{{Cite web |title=Oxalis stricta (Yellow Wood Sorrel) |url=http://www.kingdomplantae.net/yellowWoodSorrel.php |access-date=2024-04-24 |website=www.kingdomplantae.net |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061002034713/http://www.kingdomplantae.net/yellowWoodSorrel.php |archive-date=2006-10-02}}</ref> and generally requires dry or moist, [[alkali]]ne [[soil]]s, preferring [[sand]]y and [[loam]]y dirt to grow in. It requires well-drained soil and can grow in nutritionally poor grounds.

Commonly considered a [[weed]] of gardens, fields, and lawns, it grows in full sun or shade.

== Description ==
Upright yellow woodsorrel is an [[Annual plant|annual]] or short-lived [[perennial plant]] that has short [[rhizome]]s, but never has bulbs.{{sfn|Nesom|2020}} The alternate leaves of this plant are divided into three distinctively [[Heart (symbol)|heart]]-shaped leaflets (a typical trait of other species of ''[[Oxalis]])'' that can grow up to {{cvt|2|cm}} wide. These leaves curl up at night (exhibiting [[nyctinasty]]), and open in the day to perform [[photosynthesis]].

The flowers of the plant are [[hermaphroditic]], [[Blossom|blooming]] from July to October.

The mature [[seed]] capsules open explosively when disturbed (a very similar trait to that of the mature seed capsules or [[fruit]]s of plants found in the genus ''[[Impatiens]]'') and can disperse seeds up to {{cvt|4|m}} away.

Erect when young, this plant later becomes [[decumbent]] as it lies down, and branches regularly.

It is not to be confused with similar plants in the same genus which are also often referred to as "yellow woodsorrel".

==Taxonomy==
''Oxalis stricta'' was given its scientific name in 1753 by [[Carl Linnaeus]]. It is classified in the genus ''[[Oxalis]]'' within the family [[Oxalidaceae]]. It has {{table row counter|id=Synonyms}} [[Synonym (botany)|synonyms]] including 29 species names.{{sfn|POWO 2025}}

===Names===
''Oxalis stricta'' is known by the [[common name]] ''common yellow woodsorrel'',{{sfn|Everitt|Lonard|Little|2007|p=118}} also spelled ''common yellow wood-sorrel'' and ''common yellow wood sorrel'',{{sfn|Clemants|Gracie|2006|p=176}}{{sfn|Perkins|1982|p=115}} but this name has also been applied to ''[[Oxalis dillenii]]''.{{sfn|Darbyshire|Favreau|Murray|2000|p=75}} Additionally it is called ''yellow sheepsorrel'',{{sfn|Everitt|Lonard|Little|2007|p=118}} ''sheep shower'',{{sfn|Young|1993|p=58}} and ''stickwort''.{{sfn|Ferrie et al. 2015|p=45}}

It is known as ''sour grass'' for the agreeably sour flavor of the leaves and unripe pods.{{sfn|Stack|1913|p=142}} Similarly, it is informally called ''sour clover'', ''sauerkraut'', and ''pickles'', particularly by children.{{sfn|Young|1993|p=59}} Other sour names include ''sour trefoil'', ''wood sour'',{{sfn|Ferrie et al. 2015|p=45}} ''pickel plant'', and ''lemon clover''.{{sfn|Sampson|2013|p=354}} For the shape of its seed capsule it is sometimes named ''sour bananas''.{{sfn|Young|1993|p=59}}

In the early 1900s it was called ''lady's sorrel'' in the United States,{{sfn|Stack|1913|p=142}} however both ''[[Oxalis corniculata]]'' and ''[[Oxalis acetosella]]'' are also known as lady's sorrel.{{sfn|Lovelock|1972|pp=220–221}} It was also known as ''upright yellow wood-sorrel'', ''sheep sorrel'', and ''sheep poison'' around the same time in the US.{{sfn|Lyons|1900|p=271}}

==Uses==
===Culinary===
[[Image:Warming-Skudbygning-Fig21-Oxalis-stricta.jpg|thumb|A drawing showing various parts of young ''O. stricta'' plants]]

All parts of the plant are edible,<ref name=pfaf1 /> with a distinct tangy flavor (common to all plants in the genus ''[[Oxalis]]''). The leaves have a similar taste to lemons. Oxalis stricta is often eaten while hiking or camping. However, it should only be eaten in small quantities, since [[oxalic acid]] is an [[antinutrient]] and can inhibit the body's absorption of calcium.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://practicalplants.org/wiki/Oxalis_stricta|title=Oxalis stricta (Yellow Wood Sorrel) - Practical Plants|website=practicalplants.org|access-date=2016-08-02}}</ref> The sour flavor is eliminated when the plant is cooked.{{sfn|Young|1993|p=59}}

[[Image:Oxalis stricta0.jpg|thumb|''Oxalis stricta'', showing seed pods.]]
The leaves and flowers of the plant are sometimes added to salads for decoration and flavoring. These can also be chewed raw (along with other parts of the plant, but not the [[root]]) as a thirst-quencher.<ref name=pfaf1 /> The green [[Fruit|pods]] are pleasant raw, having a juicy crisp texture and a tartness similar to [[rhubarb]] in flavor.

The leaves can be used to make a flavored drink that is similar in taste to lemonade,<ref name=pfaf1 /> and the whole plant can be [[Steeping|brewed]] as [[herbal tea]] that has an aroma somewhat like that of cooked [[green beans]].

The juices of the plant have been extracted from its greens as a substitute for common [[vinegar]].
===Medicinal===
''Oxalis stricta'' contains large amounts of [[vitamin C]],<ref name="kingdomplantae"/> and has been used to treat [[scurvy]].<ref name="iastate">{{Cite web |title=Wood Sorrel |url=https://naturalresources.extension.iastate.edu/encyclopedia/wood-sorrel |access-date=2025-05-17 |website=Natural Resource Stewardship |publisher=Iowa State University |quote=}}</ref>

A [[poultice]] of the plant has been used to treat [[Swelling (medical)|swellings]].<ref name=pfaf1 />

===Practical===
An orange [[dye]] can be obtained by boiling the whole plant.<ref name=pfaf1 /><ref name="iastate"/>
